messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Cold Temperature: Cold, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Vignette:
Katherine sits rigidly, her hands clasped so tightly in her lap that her knuckles are white. For a woman who commands a tactical aircraft for a living, she appears profoundly out of her element. It has been six months since her tour as a volunteer relief worker, a mission she undertook between deployments, and the world has not felt right since. The incident itself is a memory that feels both impossibly distant and more vivid than the therapy room she now sits in. She remembers the cold most of all—a deep, biting cold that seemed to seep into her bones as her convoy distributed blankets and food in a snow-dusted, war-torn village. She remembers the sound of an approaching car, its engine labouring in the thin, frigid air. A part of her, the pilot trained in threat assessment, registered the vehicle’s speed as anomalous. But she was not a pilot that day. She was a helper. She hesitated, and in that moment of hesitation, the world dissolved into a concussive blast of heat, noise, and blinding white snow.

When she tries to speak of it now, the words simply are not there. She can picture the scene, the sequence of events, but articulating it feels like trying to grasp smoke. At other times, the memory plays out with a sterile detachment; she can recall every detail with chilling clarity but feels nothing, as if she’s watching a poorly made film about a stranger’s life. Back home, the remnants of that day have woven themselves into the fabric of her existence. The sound of a car idling too long at a stoplight on her way to the base can cause a surge of adrenaline so intense she has to pull over. The first cold snap of autumn sent her into a panic that she could not explain to her husband, Mark. Waking up is often the worst part. The nightmares leave behind a residue of terror, a physical sensation of cold on her skin that lingers long after she’s awake. In those pre-dawn hours, she finds herself creeping through her own home, checking locks, listening for the faintest sound that might signal an intruder, her pilot’s situational awareness now a prison of hypervigilance.

Over the months, Katherine has constructed a life of careful avoidance. The television remains off, as she cannot bear the risk of a news report or a film depicting anything similar to what she witnessed. Her world has shrunk to the familiar routes between home and the airbase. She has come to believe that the world is no longer a place of logic or safety, that its fundamental rules have been rewritten into something malevolent and unpredictable. This conviction makes every interaction fraught with danger; a stranger walking towards her on the sidewalk is not a fellow citizen but a potential threat, and she will cross the street abruptly to avoid them. The confident, decisive woman who once thrived on calculated risk feels like a ghost. She looks in the mirror and no longer recognizes the person staring back. Who is this frightened woman, so untethered from her own identity?

To quiet the relentless loop of self-blame—the endless rumination over her split-second of hesitation—she has found a temporary salve in impulsive online shopping. Packages arrive daily, filled with expensive cycling gear and high-end electronics, their contents often left in the box. The brief thrill of the purchase is the only time the noise in her head subsides. Mark has started to notice the credit card bills, another crack in the foundation of the life they built. The meaning she once found in her demanding career, in her marriage, in her own principles, has evaporated. Nothing feels real or important anymore. She came to therapy after a routine flight simulation last week. An auditory cue in the program—the sound of a ground vehicle—triggered a flashback so intense she lost control of the virtual aircraft. The failure, even in a simulation, was terrifying. It was a stark signal that the fortress she had built around herself was collapsing, and that she was losing the last piece of her old self she had left: the pilot. She is here now because she is afraid of what will happen when there is nothing left of the woman she used to be.
